lessons.title: What an add-on is and how to read a recommendation about it
lessons.objective: Define what an add-on is, interpret the four recommendation phrases of the 2023 ESHRE document, appraise the quality of evidence with live birth as the main outcome, and apply its messages on patient information, costs and research.
lessons.closing: An add-on is judged by live births, safety and cost, not by plausibility; what has not shown benefit should be offered only within a study, and the patient has the right to know this before paying.

lessons.title: Laboratory and stimulation: ICSI, PGT-A, time-lapse, assisted hatching, hyaluronic acid and adjuncts
lessons.objective: Apply ESHRE and NICE recommendations on ICSI without male factor, PGT-A, time-lapse imaging, assisted hatching, hyaluronic acid transfer medium and adjuncts during ovarian stimulation (growth hormone, DHEA, testosterone, antioxidants).
lessons.closing: ICSI only with an indication, PGT-A and time-lapse without proven live-birth benefit, no assisted hatching; hyaluronic acid is the “recommended” exception (benefit seen only in fresh transfers, with a single embryo), and stimulation adjuncts are not recommended routinely.

lessons.title: Endometrium and immunology: ERA, scratching, NK cells, immunomodulators and “regenerative” therapies
lessons.objective: Explain why ESHRE and NICE advise against endometrial receptivity testing, endometrial scratching, NK-cell testing and immunomodulating treatments, know the position on PRP, G-CSF and stem cells, and distinguish where the two bodies agree and where they differ.
lessons.closing: After failed transfers, the “endometrium + immunology” package has no support: no ERA, no NK testing, no intralipid, no steroids, no scratching; ESHRE and NICE agree on almost everything, and where they differ it is in the strength of the wording, not the direction.

items.title: What an add-on is: something added to standard treatment, almost always at extra cost
items.core: ESHRE calls add-ons the supplementary options offered in addition to standard fertility procedures, typically at an additional cost: tests, drugs, equipment, complementary or alternative therapies, laboratory procedures and surgical interventions. They share the stated aim of increasing pregnancy or live birth, reducing miscarriage or shortening time to pregnancy, and evidence on their safety and efficacy is often limited or lacking. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body:
Context decides: in some settings ICSI is only performed when indicated (diagnosed male factor or fertilisation failure in a previous IVF cycle) and in others it is used for all couples; in the latter, ESHRE considers ICSI an add-on, particularly if extra costs are charged. Likewise, time-lapse imaging used for research, teaching or quality control is not considered an add-on if there is no additional cost to the patient. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

Why they spread: the real risk of a cycle failing, combined with cost, leads some patients to drop out and others to look for presumed better options; and professionals may be driven by the wish to do their best, pressure from patients and sometimes competitive or commercial motives. As a benchmark for expectations, the European data cited by the document give delivery rates per fresh transfer of 26.1% with IVF and 23.9% with ICSI. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.recall: What features do add-ons share according to ESHRE, and why can ICSI be standard in one clinic and an add-on in another?
items.pearl: The same technique can be standard or an add-on depending on who it is used for and whether it is charged separately: always ask “for which patient and for which outcome?”.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023 good practice recommendations (GPR) on add-ons: review of the literature published up to 10 Aug 2022 plus working-group consensus; not a GRADE guideline and does not set a standard of care.

items.title: ESHRE’s four phrases: from “recommended” to “not recommended”
items.core: ESHRE words its 42 recommendations with four standard phrases. “Recommended”: can be applied to most patients or to the groups for whom it is relevant. “Can be considered”: can be applied after a thorough discussion of benefits and risks, with close monitoring and evaluation. “Currently not recommended for routine clinical use”: not to be applied routinely at this stage, although this may change with more evidence and it can optionally be applied to a specific group. “Not recommended”: because of safety concerns, lack of efficacy or lack of biological rationale, it should not be applied to patients and can only be evaluated in strict research settings. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body:
Examples from the document itself. “Recommended”: adding hyaluronic acid to the transfer medium; artificial oocyte activation for complete activation failure (0% 2PN), very low fertilisation (< 30%) or globozoospermia; artificial sperm activation for primary or secondary total asthenozoospermia not caused by axonemal structure defects. “Can be considered”: microfluidics for sperm selection and preparation, and screening hysteroscopy in recurrent implantation failure. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

“Currently not recommended for routine clinical use”: PGT-A, endometrial scratching, sperm DNA damage testing, KIR/HLA genotyping, IMSI, MACS, elective freeze-all and screening hysteroscopy in general. “Not recommended”: endometrial receptivity tests, peripheral blood immune tests and uterine NK testing, immunomodulating treatments, glucocorticoids, assisted hatching, ICSI without male factor, antioxidants, intrauterine or intraovarian PRP and stimulation adjuncts. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.recall: What is the practical difference between “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” and “not recommended” in the ESHRE document?
items.pearl: These four phrases are not GRADE grades (strong/weak with ⊕): they are a scale specific to a good practice document. Do not mix them up when comparing with other guidelines.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023, Table 1 (definitions of the four phrases) and Tables 2, 4 and 5 (summary of recommendations). Search up to 10 Aug 2022.

items.title: How to appraise an add-on: biological rationale, live birth, safety and cost
items.core: ESHRE took live birth (cumulative when available) as the primary outcome and used pregnancy rate only when live birth was not reported. Of its 42 recommendations, none rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence; the rest rely on low-quality trials, observational data, professional experience or consensus (the document’s abstract puts this at 95%, although 38 of 42 is 90%). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body:
Warning signs illustrated by the document itself: an effect that disappears when only trials at low risk of bias are kept (screening hysteroscopy before IVF: live-birth RR 1.26 overall, 0.99 in the 2 RCTs at low risk of bias); surrogate outcomes instead of pregnancy (semen parameters or DNA fragmentation index in antioxidant studies); small studies concentrated in a single research group (intrauterine PRP), with one RCT registered for 30 patients per arm and published with a sample more than ten times larger; and benefits that appear only in subgroups. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

ESHRE adds that several tests and interventions lack a scientific rationale or rest on questionable or incorrect theoretical foundations, and asks that they be evaluated for efficacy, safety, relevance and cost-effectiveness. For many add-ons cumulative live birth would be the optimal outcome, but it is seldom reported. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.recall: Which outcome did ESHRE use to judge add-on efficacy, and how many of its 42 recommendations rest on high-quality evidence?
items.pearl: Four questions for any add-on: does it have a biological rationale? does it increase live birth in well-conducted RCTs? what are its risks? how much does it cost and who pays?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023: abstract (limitations), methods and discussion. The hysteroscopy figures come from the Cochrane review summarised in the document.

items.title: Honest counselling: what is unproven belongs in research
items.core: ESHRE asks that every test or intervention be evaluated for efficacy, safety, relevance and cost-effectiveness, and that sharing this evaluation become a standard part of counselling. A clear distinction must be made between what has shown benefit and what has not; the latter should only be provided in a research context, and only evidence-based add-ons should be offered in clinical practice. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body:
Research means ethical approval, a clearly defined protocol and long-term follow-up. The document acknowledges that this is not always feasible (few patients, rare conditions, lack of funding) and makes clinics responsible for monitoring and following up non-established interventions and sharing results with other clinics. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

The stated aim is for patients to make informed decisions with realistic expectations, knowing the options and the likelihood that an additional test or treatment improves their chance of a live birth. ESHRE stresses that it does not intend to discourage research: for add-ons with a clear rationale, it encourages further study. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.recall: According to ESHRE, in what context should add-ons without proven benefit be offered, and what should counselling include?
items.pearl: Useful phrase: “This test has not been shown to increase your chances of having a baby; if you want it, the honest way is within a study and knowing what it costs.”

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023, abstract (implications) and discussion. Consensus position, not a graded recommendation.

items.stem: In the 2023 ESHRE document, endometrial scratching is listed as “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”. What does this phrase mean?

options.text: That it has safety concerns or lacks a biological rationale and can only be evaluated in strict research settings.
options.why: That is the definition of “not recommended”, the most restrictive category of the scale.

options.text: That it should not be applied routinely at this stage, that this may change with more evidence and that it can optionally be applied to a specific group.
options.why: Correct: this is the definition in Table 1 of the document.

options.text: That it can be applied after a thorough discussion of benefits and risks, with close monitoring and evaluation.
options.why: That is the definition of “can be considered”.

options.text: That it is a weak GRADE recommendation based on ⊕ evidence.
options.why: The four phrases are a scale specific to a good practice document, not GRADE grades.

items.explanation: The four phrases run from “recommended” to “not recommended”; “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” leaves the door open to new evidence and specific groups, unlike “not recommended”.

items.stem: A laboratory presents a new add-on with several studies. Following ESHRE’s approach, which piece of data would be most relevant to decide whether to offer it?

options.text: A higher implantation rate per transfer in a subgroup of a single-centre study.
options.why: Implantation is not the primary outcome, and benefits limited to subgroups are a warning sign (for example, with scratching, subgroup analyses failed to identify who benefits).

options.text: An improvement in laboratory parameters (for example, the sperm DNA fragmentation index).
options.why: It is a surrogate outcome; ESHRE specifically criticises antioxidant studies for using semen parameters or fragmentation instead of pregnancy.

options.text: RCTs measuring live birth, ideally cumulative, with an effect that holds in the studies at low risk of bias.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE used live birth (cumulative when available) as the primary outcome; the hysteroscopy example shows how an effect can disappear when only RCTs at low risk of bias are kept.

options.text: A plausible biological rationale described in laboratory studies.
options.why: A rationale is necessary, but ESHRE warns against premature implementation of innovations without proven safety and efficacy.

items.explanation: What matters to the patient is a baby at home: live birth in sound RCTs, plus safety and cost. Plausibility and intermediate outcomes are not enough.

items.stem: A patient (fictional case) asks for an intervention without proven live-birth benefit and says she is willing to pay for it. According to ESHRE, what is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Offer it, because the patient pays and consents.
options.why: ESHRE asks that only evidence-based add-ons be offered in clinical practice; paying does not change the evidence.

options.text: Offer it if it is cheap and seems harmless.
options.why: ESHRE asks for evaluation of efficacy, safety, relevance and cost-effectiveness; being cheap does not demonstrate benefit.

options.text: Explain the evidence and the real likelihood of benefit and, if appropriate, offer it only within a study with ethical approval, protocol and follow-up.
options.why: Correct: sharing the evaluation is part of counselling, and what is unproven should only be provided in a research context.

options.text: Refuse to discuss it so as not to raise expectations.
options.why: ESHRE aims for informed decisions with realistic expectations, which requires discussing it, not avoiding it.

items.explanation: Informing is not selling: ESHRE separates the proven from the unproven and reserves the latter for research.

items.title: ICSI without male factor: no better live birth and higher cost
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend ICSI for non-male factor infertility (“not recommended”), and its unexplained infertility guideline does not recommend it over conventional IVF (strong, ⊕). NICE advises not to use ICSI for non-male factor fertility problems if semen parameters are normal (1.50.3). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
ICSI use rose from 35% of cycles in 1997 to over 70% in 2018, even though the incidence of male factor remained stable. In an RCT of 1064 couples without male factor, ICSI gave comparable live birth (RR 1.11; 95% CI 0.93–1.32) and comparable fertilisation failure (RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.53–1.38). No clear benefit has been shown in poor responders, advanced maternal age or unexplained infertility either. It requires more laboratory time and one cost analysis estimated it to be 8.3% more expensive; perinatal outcomes appear comparable. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

Where it does fit: NICE offers ICSI with surgically retrieved sperm or frozen–thawed oocytes (1.50.1) and suggests considering it with abnormal semen parameters, taking severity into account, or after failed or very low fertilisation in a previous IVF cycle (1.50.2). NICE also advises against IMSI as an adjunct to ICSI (1.50.4) and against PICSI in preference to standard ICSI (1.50.5). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What did the 1064-couple RCT without male factor show when comparing ICSI with conventional IVF, and when does NICE suggest considering ICSI?
items.pearl: With a normal semen analysis, conventional IVF is the choice: “just in case” ICSI adds cost, not live births.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023: “not recommended”. ESHRE unexplained infertility 2023, rec. 42: strong, ⊕ (ESHRE GRADE scale: ⊕ very low, ⊕⊕ low, ⊕⊕⊕ moderate, ⊕⊕⊕⊕ high; strength and quality are different things). NICE NG257 1.50.1–1.50.5 [2026].

items.title: PGT-A: it selects embryos, it does not improve the cohort
items.core: ESHRE considers PGT-A “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”: most RCTs did not show more live births, although some suggest fewer miscarriages, and its harms include disposal of viable embryos and a possible increase in intrauterine growth restriction. NICE advises not to offer PGT-A as part of fertility treatment to improve live birth rates (1.48.1). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
The idea is reasonable: embryonic chromosomal abnormalities are common and depend on maternal age. But the Cornelisse meta-analysis found no increase in live birth after the first transfer per woman randomised, and a large Chinese RCT in women aged 20–37 also did not improve live birth per cycle. There is consensus that live birth is not the best measure for PGT-A, because it cannot improve the cohort, only select from it; yet the two RCTs that measured time to pregnancy found no difference. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

Cost and safety: it is expensive, requires specialised staff and the cost is often passed on to the patient; models suggest it might lower costs in specific groups, such as advanced maternal age with many blastocysts. Laboratories differ in diagnosing mosaicism and standardisation is lacking, with a risk of discarding viable embryos because of analytical errors. NICE adds that it can leave no embryo to transfer in that cycle and that emerging evidence on fewer miscarriages coexists with major uncertainties. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Why can PGT-A not increase the number of live births from a cohort, and what do ESHRE and NICE say about its routine use?
items.pearl: PGT-A does not create euploid embryos: it only chooses among those available. If someone promises “more babies”, ask for cumulative live birth per woman, not per transfer.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023: “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”. NICE NG257 1.48.1 [2026].

items.title: Time-lapse and assisted hatching: no more live births
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend time-lapse imaging as a tool to improve live birth, nor assisted hatching (“not recommended”). NICE advises not to offer assisted hatching because it has not been shown to improve pregnancy rates (1.49.1, from 2004) and made no recommendation on time-lapse for embryo selection. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
Time-lapse: the Cochrane review summarised by ESHRE found no difference in live birth or ongoing pregnancy (OR 0.91; 95% CI 0.67–1.23; 3 RCTs; n = 826; low quality). Selection algorithms appear to be laboratory dependent. It is useful for research, teaching, standardisation and quality control, but many clinics advertise it as improving outcomes and some charge extra for it. NICE found no benefit in pregnancy or live birth (very low certainty) but did not want to preclude its use because of possible benefits of stable incubation. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Assisted hatching: in the Cochrane review, no significant effect on live birth (OR 1.09; 95% CI 0.92–1.29; 14 RCTs; n = 2849; low quality), with a slight increase in clinical pregnancy (OR 1.20; 95% CI 1.09–1.33; 39 RCTs; low quality). There is concern about a possible increase in multiple pregnancy and monozygotic twinning, though with too few cases to conclude. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.recall: What do ESHRE and NICE recommend on time-lapse imaging and assisted hatching, and how does their position on time-lapse differ?
items.pearl: A time-lapse incubator can be good laboratory equipment; what is not proven is that paying for it brings more babies.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023: time-lapse “not recommended” as a tool to improve live birth; assisted hatching “not recommended”. NICE NG257 1.49.1 [2004]; no recommendation on time-lapse (rationale for 1.48.1).

items.title: Hyaluronic acid in the transfer medium: the “recommended” add-on, with small print
items.core: ESHRE recommends adding hyaluronic acid to the transfer medium (“recommended”) and advises continued monitoring of the multiple pregnancy rate; its use should be combined with a single embryo transfer policy. The benefit was seen in fresh transfers, not frozen ones. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body:
In the Cochrane review (26 RCTs; 6704 women), a high concentration of hyaluronic acid (0.5 mg/ml) increased live birth compared with a low concentration or none (RR 1.21; 10 RCTs; n = 4066; moderate quality; number needed to treat 14), for both cleavage-stage and blastocyst transfers and for good and poor prognosis patients. In 3 of 8 studies with exposure under 10 minutes there was no effect. In frozen transfers (3 studies; n = 713) there was no benefit, and an RCT of 550 frozen cycles also found none; in donor oocyte cycles the effect was small (RR 1.12; 2 RCTs; n = 317; low quality). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

Safety: multiple pregnancy increased (RR 1.45; 95% CI 1.24–1.70; 7 RCTs; n = 3337; moderate quality), attributed to transferring more than one embryo with high-concentration hyaluronic acid; there were no more miscarriages, ectopic pregnancies or malformations. Other “adherence” compounds (albumin, fibrin, collagen) have no evidence of benefit. We found no recommendation on this add-on in the text of NICE NG257. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: In which type of transfer did high-concentration hyaluronic acid show a benefit, and which risk requires combining it with a single embryo?
items.pearl: It is the only clinical-management add-on with the “recommended” phrase in the ESHRE document; the recommendation does not specify the type of transfer, but the benefit was seen only in fresh transfers, and it should be combined with a single embryo.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023: “recommended”, with monitoring of multiple pregnancy and single embryo transfer. The quality grades (moderate/low) are those assigned by the summarised Cochrane review. NICE NG257 does not address it.

items.title: Growth hormone, DHEA, testosterone and antioxidants during stimulation
items.core: ESHRE (add-ons, 2023) does not recommend adjuncts before or during stimulation (metformin, growth hormone, testosterone, DHEA, aspirin, indomethacin and sildenafil), nor antioxidants in ART. Its 2025 ovarian stimulation guideline gives more detail: growth hormone not recommended in normal responders (strong, ⊕) or PCOS (strong, ⊕⊕) and probably not recommended in low responders (conditional, ⊕); testosterone probably not recommended in low responders (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕); DHEA not recommended in low or normal responders (strong, ⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]]
items.body:
Growth hormone in low responders: the 2025 guideline acknowledges that the updated Cochrane review and a 2025 meta-analysis suggest more live births, but judges the evidence to be of too limited quality (underpowered studies and very heterogeneous definitions of low response), recalls that it has the potential for serious harm and that there are no long-term safety data, and encourages research. Aspirin is not recommended in the general IVF/ICSI population or in low responders (strong, ⊕⊕⊕), nor sildenafil in low responders (strong, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]]

The add-ons document points to serious safety concerns with some adjuncts, such as sildenafil, and leaves room for research in specific circumstances. On antioxidants: uncertain effect on live birth in women, no evidence in men, with gastrointestinal discomfort reported; the unexplained infertility guideline considers them probably not recommended for women undergoing treatment (conditional, ⊕). NICE refers to the 2025 ESHRE stimulation guideline for pre-treatment (1.40). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What does the 2025 ESHRE stimulation guideline say about growth hormone and DHEA in low responders, and with what strength?
items.pearl: In low responders, growth hormone is the greyest case: possible benefit, weak evidence and unknown long-term safety. That is “probably not”, not “yes”.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023: “not recommended” (based on the 2020 stimulation guideline). ESHRE ovarian stimulation 2025, rec. 46 [2025] strong ⊕; 47 [updated] conditional ⊕; 48 [2025] strong ⊕⊕; 49 [updated] conditional ⊕⊕⊕; 50 [2019] and 51 [2025] strong ⊕⊕; 52 [2019] strong ⊕⊕⊕; 53 [2019] strong ⊕. ESHRE unexplained infertility 2023, rec. 46: conditional ⊕. ⊕ scale: very low up to ⊕⊕⊕⊕ high.

items.stem: A couple (fictional case) with unexplained infertility and a normal semen analysis is about to start IVF. The clinic proposes ICSI “to secure fertilisation”. What is most appropriate according to ESHRE and NICE?

options.text: Conventional IVF, because ICSI without male factor does not improve live birth.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE does not recommend it without male factor or in unexplained infertility (strong, ⊕), and NICE advises against it with normal semen parameters (1.50.3).

options.text: ICSI, because in a large RCT without male factor it increased live birth.
options.why: In the 1064-couple RCT live birth was comparable (RR 1.11; 95% CI 0.93–1.32).

options.text: ICSI combined with IMSI to select sperm better.
options.why: NICE advises against IMSI as an adjunct to ICSI (1.50.4), and ESHRE does not recommend it routinely.

options.text: ICSI only if the woman is over 39.
options.why: In advanced maternal age ICSI did not improve fertilisation or clinical outcomes; the RCT in women over 39 found comparable fertilisation rates and numbers of top-quality embryos.

items.explanation: Without male factor or previous fertilisation failure, ICSI adds cost and laboratory time without more live births.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman (fictional case) asks whether adding PGT-A to her next IVF cycle will increase her chance of having a baby. Which answer best fits ESHRE and NICE?

options.text: Yes: by discarding aneuploid embryos it increases cumulative live birth per cycle.
options.why: PGT-A cannot improve the cohort, only select from it; most RCTs showed no more live births.

options.text: It has not been shown to increase live birth; it can leave fewer embryos to transfer, and ESHRE does not recommend it routinely while NICE advises not to offer it for that purpose.
options.why: Correct: “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” (ESHRE) and NICE 1.48.1.

options.text: Yes, because it has been shown to shorten time to pregnancy.
options.why: The two RCTs that measured time to pregnancy found no difference.

options.text: It is harmless and standardised, so there is no downside to adding it.
options.why: There is a lack of standardisation between laboratories, a risk of discarding viable embryos and a possible increase in intrauterine growth restriction, plus the cost.

items.explanation: PGT-A selects, it does not create euploid embryos: its live-birth benefit is unproven and it carries costs and risks of discarding.

items.stem: A patient (fictional case) is having a frozen embryo transfer and asks for “embryo glue” and two embryos to increase her chances. What is most correct according to ESHRE?

options.text: Accept both, because hyaluronic acid is “recommended” for any transfer.
options.why: The benefit was seen in fresh transfers; there was none in frozen transfers, and combining it with two embryos increases multiple pregnancy.

options.text: Explain that no benefit was shown in frozen transfers and that, when used, it should be combined with a single embryo because of the increase in multiple pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: no benefit in frozen transfers (3 studies and an RCT of 550 cycles) and increased multiple pregnancy (RR 1.45), which is why ESHRE asks for single embryo transfer.

options.text: Use albumin or fibrin as an alternative adherence compound.
options.why: Studies of albumin, fibrin or collagen are scarce and show no increase in implantation or live births.

options.text: Add assisted hatching to compensate.
options.why: Assisted hatching is “not recommended” (ESHRE) and NICE advises against offering it (1.49.1).

items.explanation: Hyaluronic acid is the only clinical-management add-on with the “recommended” phrase, but the benefit was seen only in fresh transfers and ESHRE asks for it to be combined with a single embryo. In frozen transfers no benefit has been shown, whereas the multiple-pregnancy risk is real.

items.stem: A low responder (fictional case) asks about adding growth hormone, DHEA or testosterone to her next stimulation. Which statement is correct according to the 2025 ESHRE ovarian stimulation guideline?

options.text: Growth hormone is strongly recommended in low responders.
options.why: It is “probably not recommended” in low responders (conditional, ⊕), because of limited-quality evidence and unknown long-term safety.

options.text: DHEA is the alternative of choice if growth hormone is not used.
options.why: DHEA is not recommended in low responders (strong, ⊕⊕).

options.text: Growth hormone is probably not recommended (conditional, ⊕), although meta-analyses suggest a possible live-birth benefit with limited-quality evidence.
options.why: Correct: this is rec. 47 and its justification (underpowered studies, heterogeneous definitions, potential for serious harm and no long-term safety data).

options.text: Testosterone is recommended before stimulation in low responders.
options.why: Testosterone is probably not recommended in low responders (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕).

items.explanation: None of the three adjuncts is recommended; growth hormone stays at “probably not” because of a possible benefit with weak evidence, and the add-ons document groups them as “not recommended”.

items.title: Endometrial receptivity tests (ERA and similar): no
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend the currently available endometrial receptivity tests (“not recommended”). NICE advises not to offer endometrial receptivity testing as an add-on for embryo transfer, including gene expression analysis (for example, ERA) and microbiological analysis (endometrial microbiome, infectious chronic endometritis) (1.41.1). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
The largest RCT (double blind, 30 US sites, 767 women with at least one frozen euploid blastocyst) did not improve live birth by timing transfer according to the test: 58.5% vs 61.9% (RR 0.95; 95% CI 0.79–1.13). An earlier RCT showed no effect in the intention-to-treat analysis, and a multicentre cohort of 5372 transfers found fewer live births after testing and personalised transfer than with fresh transfer. ESHRE adds that the tests do not capture the interplay between endometrium and embryo, nor the timing, location and depth of the biopsy, which can be painful. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

NICE found no difference in clinical pregnancy or live birth; ERA-timed transfer had less multiple gestation than standard fresh transfer but more clinical pregnancy loss. Because there is no evidence on treating microbiome abnormalities, it made a research recommendation (for example, antibiotics for endometritis or microbiota transplantation). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What did the 767-woman RCT with euploid blastocysts show about receptivity-guided transfer, and what does the NICE recommendation include?
items.pearl: With euploid blastocysts, adjusting the transfer day according to the test did not bring more babies: it is the “cleanest” possible scenario and it still did not work.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023: “not recommended”. NICE NG257 1.41.1 [2026] and research recommendation 1 [2026].

items.title: Endometrial scratching: 37 RCTs and still no clear benefit
items.core: ESHRE considers endometrial scratching “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”, and its unexplained infertility guideline states it should not be offered (strong, ⊕⊕). NICE advises not to offer it as a pre-treatment to improve IVF outcome (1.40.1). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
The most recent Cochrane review included 37 RCTs (8786 women); in the main analysis, restricted to studies at low risk of bias, the effect on live birth was unclear, consistent with no effect, a small reduction or an improvement (OR 1.12; 95% CI 0.98–1.28; 8 RCTs; n = 4402; moderate quality), and probably little or no effect on miscarriage. In the first IVF cycle there was no effect (RR 1.04; 95% CI 0.89–1.21; n = 1048). Some subgroups (for example, scratching twice after previous failure) gave positive results, but another review found no difference in any group, and ESHRE concludes that subgroup analyses failed to identify who benefits. It may cause minimal to moderate pain and bleeding (and a small risk of infection if done by hysteroscopy); one study estimated €6524 per additional live birth. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

NICE reasons that the evidence is inconsistent (possible harm, possible benefit or no effect) and that it is an invasive procedure with time, resource and financial costs, because it cannot be combined with another procedure. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What did the 37-RCT Cochrane review conclude about scratching and live birth, and what do ESHRE and NICE recommend?
items.pearl: When dozens of RCTs cannot find a clear effect, searching for “the subgroup that responds” is usually noise, not signal.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023: “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”. ESHRE unexplained infertility 2023, rec. 45: strong, ⊕⊕. NICE NG257 1.40.1 [2026].

items.title: “NK cells reject the embryo”: immune tests and treatments without a basis
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend peripheral blood immune tests or uterine NK-cell testing (“not recommended”), considers KIR/HLA genotyping “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”, and does not recommend immunomodulating treatments (intralipid, IVIG, rh-LIF, PBMCs, anti-TNF) or glucocorticoids in ART. NICE advises not to use immunological agents, including intralipids, intravenous immunoglobulins and steroids, as part of fertility treatment (1.42.1). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
The myth: the fetus would be “rejected” and uterine NK cells could kill it. ESHRE calls this incorrect: the placenta always separates the fetus from the maternal immune system, and uterine NK cells are only weakly cytolytic and cannot kill placental cells. The proportion of NK cells in blood varies widely in healthy people (5–25%), clinics’ cut-offs are arbitrary, and uterine populations differ from those in blood; a meta-analysis found no difference in live birth between high and normal uterine NK cells (RR 1.00; 95% CI 0.77–1.28; 3 studies; n = 229). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

Treatments: intralipid, uncertain effect (RR 1.78; 95% CI 0.95–3.34; 2 RCTs; 244 patients); IVIG, a single RCT of 51 patients with no clear effect; rh-LIF, fewer live births (RR 0.47; 95% CI 0.24–0.91). Reported adverse effects: hepatomegaly, cholestasis and fat overload syndrome with intralipid; aseptic meningitis, renal failure, thromboembolism and anaphylaxis with IVIG; malformations with tacrolimus (4 in 100 pregnancies in transplant recipients). Glucocorticoids: no difference in live birth (OR 1.08; 95% CI 0.45–2.58; 2 RCTs; n = 310; low quality), with reported increases in miscarriage, preterm birth, gestational hypertension and diabetes. NICE adds that IVIG is invasive and expensive and that steroids, by suppressing immunity, increase the risk of infection. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Why does ESHRE consider incorrect the idea that uterine NK cells kill the embryo, and what do ESHRE and NICE say about intralipid, IVIG and steroids?
items.pearl: This section does not refer to women with autoimmune disease (thyroid disease, antiphospholipid syndrome) or to those already on immune treatment for another indication: there the disease is treated, no add-on is added.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023: peripheral blood immune tests and uterine NK testing, immunomodulators and glucocorticoids “not recommended”; KIR/HLA “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”. NICE NG257 1.42.1 [2026].

items.title: PRP, G-CSF, intrauterine hCG and stem cells: “rejuvenation” without proof
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend (“not recommended”) intrauterine or intraovarian platelet-rich plasma (PRP), intrauterine G-CSF, intrauterine hCG, or stem cell therapy for premature ovarian insufficiency, diminished ovarian reserve or thin endometrium. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body:
Intrauterine PRP: a review (7 studies; n = 625) found more clinical pregnancies (RR 1.79), but with small samples, heterogeneous populations, possible overrepresentation of one research group, and an RCT registered for 30 patients per arm and published with more than ten times that sample. Intraovarian PRP: there are no RCTs; data come from one case-control study and uncontrolled studies (696 women), with no safety data on injection into the ovarian stroma. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

Intrauterine G-CSF: one review suggested more live births (RR 1.52; 95% CI 1.11–2.10; 5 RCTs) with low certainty; in implantation failure there was no significant difference (RR 1.43; 95% CI 0.86–2.36; 3 RCTs; n = 372), and the possible benefit in thin endometrium comes from a single RCT. Stem cells: there are no RCTs or comparative studies, only case series and small observational studies; ESHRE points to serious safety concerns (invasive procedures, long-term effects and risk of tumorigenesis), and there are no data on the health of children born. We found no specific recommendations on PRP, G-CSF or stem cells in the text of NICE NG257. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What methodological problems does ESHRE point out in intrauterine PRP studies, and what evidence is there for intraovarian PRP?
items.pearl: “Ovarian rejuvenation” with PRP: not a single RCT. If a patient with low reserve asks for it, the honest conversation is about evidence-based options, including donation.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023: “not recommended” for intrauterine and intraovarian PRP, intrauterine G-CSF, intrauterine hCG and stem cells. NICE NG257: no specific recommendation found.

items.title: ESHRE versus NICE: same direction, different strength
items.core: They agree on not offering endometrial receptivity tests, immunological treatments, ICSI without male factor or assisted hatching, and on not using PGT-A to improve live birth. They differ mainly in the strength of the wording: where the add-ons document says “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” (PGT-A, scratching), NICE says “do not offer”; for scratching, the ESHRE unexplained infertility guideline already says it should not be offered (strong, ⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
Other differences. Time-lapse: ESHRE does not recommend it to improve live birth; NICE made no recommendation and did not want to preclude its use because of stable incubation. Hyaluronic acid in the transfer medium: ESHRE recommends it; we found no recommendation in NICE NG257. Screening hysteroscopy: ESHRE considers it “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” but says it “can be considered” in recurrent implantation failure; NICE advises not to offer it as a pre-treatment for IVF unless uterine or endometrial abnormalities are suspected (1.40.2). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Dates and scope: the ESHRE document reviewed literature up to August 2022 and its stimulation adjuncts refer to the 2020 guideline, since updated in 2025; most NICE recommendations on add-ons date from 2026, but the one on assisted hatching dates from 2004. For pre-treatment, NICE refers to the 2025 ESHRE stimulation guideline. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation]]
items.recall: On which add-ons do ESHRE and NICE agree, and on which do they differ (time-lapse, hyaluronic acid, screening hysteroscopy)?
items.pearl: If one guideline says “not routinely” and the other “do not offer”, neither supports routine use: the difference is how much room they leave for research or specific groups.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023 (search up to 10 Aug 2022). NICE NG257: 1.40.1, 1.40.2, 1.41.1, 1.42.1, 1.48.1 and 1.50.3 [2026]; 1.49.1 [2004]. ESHRE ovarian stimulation 2025.

items.stem: After two failed transfers of good-quality frozen blastocysts (fictional case), an endometrial receptivity test is proposed to personalise the day of the next transfer. What is most correct?

options.text: Do it, because test-guided transfer increases live birth.
options.why: In the largest RCT (767 women with at least one frozen euploid blastocyst, the most favourable scenario for the test) there was no improvement (58.5% vs 61.9%; RR 0.95).

options.text: Do not do it: ESHRE does not recommend these tests and NICE advises not to offer them as an add-on for transfer.
options.why: Correct: “not recommended” (ESHRE) and NICE 1.41.1, which includes ERA and microbiological analysis.

options.text: Do it, but only with added endometrial microbiome analysis.
options.why: NICE explicitly includes microbiome analysis in the do-not-offer recommendation and only proposes research on its treatment.

options.text: Do it, since the biopsy is harmless and has no drawbacks.
options.why: The biopsy can be painful, it postpones the transfer to another cycle, and ESHRE notes that the tests do not capture endometrium–embryo interplay.

items.explanation: The most favourable scenario for the test (euploid blastocysts) showed no benefit; that is why ESHRE and NICE advise against it.

items.stem: A patient with no known autoimmune disease (fictional case) brings a blood NK-cell test her clinic considers “high” and a proposal of intralipid and prednisone for the next transfer. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Follow the proposal, because high NK cells explain implantation failure.
options.why: The proportion of blood NK cells ranges from 5% to 25% in healthy people, cut-offs are arbitrary, and they do not reflect uterine NK cells.

options.text: Replace the blood test with a uterine NK biopsy and treat if they are high.
options.why: Uterine NK testing is not recommended either: high versus normal NK cells did not change live birth (RR 1.00).

options.text: Use prednisone alone, since steroids are safe in early pregnancy.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend glucocorticoids in ART, with reported increases in miscarriage, preterm birth, gestational hypertension and diabetes; NICE advises against them.

options.text: Do not treat: neither the test nor intralipid nor steroids are recommended, and they carry risks.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE “not recommended” for blood tests, immunomodulators and glucocorticoids, and NICE 1.42.1.

items.explanation: Without diagnosed autoimmunity, measuring NK cells and treating them with immunomodulators lacks a basis and exposes the patient to adverse effects.

items.stem: A patient (fictional case) with unexplained infertility and two failed transfers asks whether endometrial scratching in the luteal phase before her next IVF cycle would help. Which answer fits best?

options.text: Yes, because after previous implantation failures it clearly increases live birth.
options.why: Not proven: in a review of women with at least one previous failure live birth improved (RR 1.18), but when restricted to those with at least two failed cycles there was no difference (RR 1.30; 95% CI 0.87–1.94), and another review found no difference in any group, including two or more failed cycles.

options.text: Yes, as long as it is done twice.
options.why: The positive result for scratching twice is a subgroup of a review focused on previous failures; ESHRE concludes that subgroups do not identify who benefits.

options.text: No: the effect on live birth is uncertain, it involves pain and cost, and ESHRE and NICE advise against offering it.
options.why: Correct: “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” (ESHRE add-ons), “should not be offered” in unexplained infertility (strong, ⊕⊕) and NICE 1.40.1.

options.text: It makes no difference: it has no adverse effects or cost, so she can have it if she wishes.
options.why: It may cause minimal to moderate pain and bleeding, and NICE stresses that it is invasive with time, resource and financial costs.

items.explanation: After 37 RCTs, scratching still has no clear live-birth benefit; all three sources agree not to offer it routinely.

items.title: Case: Noemí, Gabriel and the “full package” after two failed transfers

steps.text: Noemí (fictional case), 38, and Gabriel, 40, with no known autoimmune disease and a normal semen analysis. After IVF with two failed transfers of good-quality frozen blastocysts, a clinic offers them a paid “package”: endometrial receptivity test, NK testing with intralipid and prednisone, scratching, ICSI and PGT-A in the next cycle. ESHRE recalls that add-ons usually carry an additional cost and limited evidence, and that sharing their evaluation is part of counselling. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] They start by asking about the receptivity test.

It is explained that neither ESHRE nor NICE supports the test. Noemí then asks about NK cells: a friend “had high NK cells” and was treated with intralipid. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Immune tests and treatments are ruled out. Scratching and laboratory changes remain. ESHRE does not recommend routine scratching and NICE advises not to offer it; subgroup analyses after previous failures did not identify who benefits. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

For the new cycle, with a normal semen analysis, there is no indication for ICSI: ESHRE and NICE advise against it without male factor. Gabriel asks whether PGT-A will at least give them a better chance of having a baby. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Wrap-up: a conventional IVF cycle without the package is agreed. If they are considered to have recurrent implantation failure, ESHRE allows screening hysteroscopy as “can be considered”, whereas NICE advises not to offer it as a pre-treatment and reserves investigation for when uterine or endometrial abnormalities are suspected. If hyaluronic acid is used at the next fresh transfer, ESHRE asks for it to be combined with a single embryo. They are told that any other intervention without proven benefit should only be done within a study. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

eshre-2023-addons.title: Good practice recommendations on add-ons in reproductive medicine
eshre-2023-addons.authors: ESHRE Add-ons Working Group; Lundin K, Bentzen JG, Bozdag G, Ebner T, Harper J, Le Clef N, Moffett A, Norcross S, Polyzos NP, Rautakallio-Hokkanen S, Sfontouris I, Sermon K, Vermeulen N, Pinborg A
eshre-2023-addons.population: Patients undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART); Hum Reprod 2023 (ESHRE Pages).
eshre-2023-addons.finding: 42 recommendations using its own four-phrase scale (recommended; can be considered; currently not recommended for routine clinical use; not recommended). Peripheral blood immune tests and uterine NK-cell testing: not recommended. Screening hysteroscopy: currently not recommended for routine clinical use (can be considered in recurrent implantation failure). Sperm DNA damage testing, endometrial scratching and KIR/HLA genotyping: currently not recommended for routine clinical use. ICSI for non-male factor infertility: not recommended.
eshre-2023-addons.limitations: Full text read (UCL Discovery open-access copy of the advance online version); the wording of every cited recommendation and the scale-definition table were checked verbatim. Good practice recommendations based on review and consensus, not a GRADE guideline: no recommendation rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence. ART population, not specifically unexplained infertility.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.title: Ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI — ESHRE guideline update 2025
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Ovarian Stimulation
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.population: Women starting ovarian stimulation for IVF/ICSI.
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.finding: Recommends AFC or AMH to predict high and low response (strong). Does not recommend AFC, AMH or other basal markers to predict pregnancy or live birth (strong). Female age and BMI are predictors of pregnancy and live birth (strong). Age, BMI, FSH, inhibin B and other basal hormones should not be routinely used to predict response.
eshre-2025-ovarian-stimulation.limitations: Full guideline v23 (September 2026); journal version: Hum Reprod 2026;41(4):498-514. Certainty for each recommendation is given in the full guideline.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.
